TrialSurv evidence review

Adjuvant chemotherapy for resected colon cancer: a time-to-event re-analysis

Author

TrialSurv analysis team

Published

November 17, 2026

Executive summary

This independent re-analysis of the colon cancer adjuvant chemotherapy trial data distributed with the survival package (Moertel et al., 1990) includes 888 patients with 430 deaths and a median follow-up of 77.3 months. Adding levamisole plus fluorouracil (Lev+5FU) to surgery was associated with better overall survival than observation: the adjusted hazard ratio was 0.64 (95% CI 0.48 to 0.86) and 5-year survival was 63.6% versus 52.0% (log-rank p = 0.004). The Bayesian hierarchical model, which partially borrows information across four nodal-risk strata, gave a global hazard ratio of 0.68 (95% credible interval 0.46 to 0.98) and converged cleanly (maximum R-hat 1.0010, zero divergences). The treatment effect is consistent in direction across nodal strata, but the proportional hazards assumption is not globally satisfied. The recommendation is GO-WITH-MODIFICATION: proceed, but with a pre-specified proportional-hazards-robust analysis and a sample size justified by simulation.

What we measured

The analysis follows patients from surgery until one of two time-to-event endpoints occurs: cancer recurrence or death. For each patient we know either the time the event happened, or the time they were last known to be event-free. The latter is censoring: the patient did not have the event during follow-up, so we know only that their event time was later than their last visit. Censoring is not missing data; it is information, and survival methods use it explicitly.

The main summary is the hazard ratio (HR). A hazard is the instantaneous rate of the event at a given time among patients still event-free. An HR compares that rate between two arms at the same time. An HR of 1 means no difference; an HR below 1 means the treatment arm has a lower event rate. An HR of 0.64 means that, at any given time after surgery, the Lev+5FU arm had about 36% lower instantaneous risk of death than observation. We also report median survival (the time by which half the arm has died) and 5-year survival (the probability of being alive at 60 months). A median of “not reached” means more than half of that arm was still alive at the end of follow-up; it is a good result, not a missing value.

All times are in months. The cohort is the complete-case set used consistently by every model: patients missing a required baseline variable were excluded before analysis and the exclusion is recorded in the data loader.

Survival by treatment arm

Kaplan-Meier summary by arm, death endpoint.
Arm n Deaths Median (months) Median lower Median upper 5-year survival 5-year lower 5-year upper
Obs 305 164 68.2 50.3 83.8 52.0% 46.7% 57.9%
Lev 294 149 80.8 56.1 54.8% 49.3% 60.8%
Lev+5FU 289 117 Not reached 89.5 63.6% 58.3% 69.4%

The observation arm had a median survival of 68.2 months and 5-year survival of 52.0%. The Lev+5FU arm had not reached median survival and 5-year survival of 63.6%, a difference of 11.6 percentage points. The log-rank test comparing all three arms gave chi-square = 11.02 on 2 degrees of freedom and p = 0.004. The curves separate early and remain apart, which is why the treatment effect is not simply a late follow-up artefact.

Adjusted treatment effect

Cox proportional hazards estimates for the treatment contrasts.
Model Contrast HR 95% CI low 95% CI high p-value
unadjusted Lev vs Obs 0.97 0.75 1.27 0.839
unadjusted Lev+5FU vs Obs 0.67 0.50 0.89 0.006
adjusted Lev vs Obs 0.91 0.70 1.20 0.511
adjusted Lev+5FU vs Obs 0.64 0.48 0.86 0.003

The unadjusted hazard ratio for Lev+5FU versus observation was 0.67 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.89), and the covariate-adjusted hazard ratio was 0.64 (95% CI 0.48 to 0.86, p = 0.003). Interpretation: after accounting for age, sex, nodal involvement, extent of disease, differentiation and obstruction, patients receiving Lev+5FU had about 36% lower instantaneous risk of death than patients on observation, and the confidence interval excludes no effect. Levamisole alone was not clearly different from observation (adjusted HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.20).

The adjusted model is the primary frequentist estimate because the trial population differed on important prognostic factors. The held-out C-index for this model was 0.648 (95% CI 0.602 to 0.694) on the 30% test set, compared with 0.532 for the unadjusted model. A C-index of 0.65 means the model discriminates moderately well between patients who die sooner and later, not that it is a perfect prediction tool.

Does the proportional hazards assumption hold?

The Cox model assumes that the hazard ratio is constant over time. The Schoenfeld residual test checks this: a small p-value is evidence that an effect changes over time. The global test here gave chi-square = 29.69 with p = 0.002, so the proportional hazards assumption is not globally satisfied. The treatment term for Lev+5FU itself gave p = 0.698, which does not show a time-varying treatment effect. The violations are concentrated in other covariates: rxLev, extentMuscle, extentContiguous, differModerate, differPoor, obstruct.

What this means for trust. The Lev+5FU hazard ratio is the best single-number summary of the treatment effect and is supported by both the frequentist and Bayesian analyses, but the global test says the full Cox model is an imperfect description of the data. A non-significant treatment-specific test is reassuring; it does not prove that the treatment effect is constant. The next trial should pre-specify a time-varying or restricted-mean-survival sensitivity analysis, and the report should not present the HR as if it captures the entire survival curve. This is the main statistical reason the recommendation is conditional rather than an unqualified GO.

Bayesian subgroup analysis and partial borrowing

The Bayesian model fits a Weibull proportional hazards model with a hierarchical random effect for the Lev+5FU effect across four nodal-risk strata: 0-1, 2-3, 4-7 and 8+ positive lymph nodes. Each stratum’s log hazard ratio is shrunk toward the global Lev+5FU effect through a half-normal prior with scale 0.5. This is partial borrowing: strata with more events and more information keep most of their own estimate; small or unstable strata are pulled toward the overall effect rather than being reported as if they were independent studies. The model adjusted for age, sex, extent, differentiation and obstruction, and handled censoring through the Weibull likelihood.

Partially pooled Lev+5FU hazard ratios by nodal-risk stratum.
Parameter Posterior mean HR 95% CrI low 95% CrI high R-hat Bulk ESS
Nodes 0-1 0.69 0.46 0.99 1.000 9,073
Nodes 2-3 0.71 0.49 1.01 1.000 8,401
Nodes 4-7 0.63 0.41 0.89 1.000 8,181
Nodes 8+ 0.71 0.47 1.07 1.000 9,460

The global posterior mean hazard ratio was 0.68 (95% CrI 0.46 to 0.98), and the stratum-specific estimates ranged from 0.63 to 0.71. Every subgroup estimate is below 1 in point estimate; the upper credible limits are close to or slightly above 1 in the smaller strata, which is exactly what borrowing is meant to communicate honestly.

How far each stratum estimate moved toward the global effect.
Stratum n Deaths Standalone HR Pooled HR Absolute movement (log scale) Interval width reduction
Nodes 0-1 187 64 0.68 0.68 0.008 35.8%
Nodes 2-3 216 92 0.67 0.69 0.029 30.2%
Nodes 4-7 141 87 0.62 0.62 0.009 30.2%
Nodes 8+ 74 56 0.82 0.69 0.171 36.5%

The interval width fell by 30.2% to 36.5% after borrowing. The absolute movement was largest in the 8+ node stratum (0.171 on the log-HR scale), the smallest subgroup (74 patients). In the 2-3 node stratum the standalone estimate was already essentially the global effect, so the percentage movement is unstable and slightly negative; the absolute movement is only 0.029 and the interval still narrowed by 30.2%. The Bayesian fit converged with maximum R-hat 1.0010, minimum bulk ESS 3,311, and 0 divergent transitions (backend: brms). Trace plots are available in figures/trace.png.

Frequentist versus Bayesian comparison

Frequentist and Bayesian treatment-effect summaries on the same test set.
Model HR Interval low Interval high Interval width Held-out C-index C-index low C-index high WAIC
Frequentist (adjusted Cox) 0.64 0.48 0.86 0.38 0.648 0.602 0.694 Not available
Bayesian (hierarchical Weibull) 0.68 0.46 0.98 0.52 0.652 0.629 0.669 3372.7

The two approaches agree on the direction and approximate size of the effect. The frequentist adjusted HR is 0.64 (95% CI 0.48 to 0.86, width 0.38); the Bayesian global HR is 0.68 (95% CrI 0.46 to 0.98, width 0.52). The Bayesian interval is wider, which is appropriate: it includes the hierarchical uncertainty about how much the nodal strata differ. Held-out discrimination was essentially identical (0.648 vs 0.652). The Bayesian WAIC was 3372.7; WAIC is a relative model-fit score, not a hypothesis test, and it is reported here only for completeness.

How big does the next trial need to be?

The simulation engine randomises patients under uniform accrual, exponential control survival with a 60-month median, a proportional treatment effect, administrative censoring at 24 months of accrual plus 60 months of follow-up, and independent dropout. Each design cell uses 1,000 simulated trials. Rejection rates at HR = 1 estimate the type I error rate; at HR < 1 they estimate power.

Per-arm sample size required for 80% power (target HR 0.8 and 0.7).
HR Dropout Simulated n per arm Power at that n Schoenfeld n per arm Simulated / Schoenfeld
0.8 0% 800 90% 602 1.33
0.7 0% 300 88% 246 1.22
0.8 20% 800 86% 675 1.19
0.7 20% 300 82% 276 1.09

For a future trial targeting HR = 0.7 with 20% dropout, the simulation first reached 80% power at 300 patients per arm (observed power 82%); the Schoenfeld calculation gives 276 per arm (ratio 1.09). For HR = 0.8 with 20% dropout, the corresponding numbers are 800 and 675 per arm. Without dropout, the requirement is 300 per arm at HR = 0.7 and 800 at HR = 0.8. The simulated requirement was 9% to 33% higher than the Schoenfeld analytic size, which is a useful reality check but not a substitute for a trial-specific design.

At HR = 1, the pooled empirical type I error was 5.08% (95% MC interval 4.69% to 5.48%) across 12,000 null simulations, consistent with the nominal 5%. The total simulation run comprised 96,000 simulated trials in 2.3 minutes on 7 cores.

Recommendation

ImportantRecommendation: GO-WITH-MODIFICATION

The three numbers driving this decision

  1. Adjusted hazard ratio 0.64 (95% CI 0.48 to 0.86) for Lev+5FU versus observation, with a Bayesian global HR of 0.68 (95% CrI 0.46 to 0.98).
  2. 5-year survival 63.6% versus 52.0%, an 11.6 percentage-point absolute gain (log-rank p = 0.004).
  3. About 300 patients per arm for 80% power at HR = 0.7 with 20% dropout (Schoenfeld 276), so the next trial must be sized in the hundreds per arm, not dozens.

The three main caveats

  1. Proportional hazards is not globally satisfied (global cox.zph p = 0.002; violations in rxLev, extentMuscle, extentContiguous, differModerate, differPoor, obstruct). The treatment-specific test is not significant, but the constant-HR summary should be paired with a time-varying or restricted-mean-survival sensitivity analysis.
  2. The Bayesian subgroup intervals remain wide, especially in the 8+ node stratum (74 patients), and the borrowing is deliberately modest. Subgroup estimates should guide future stratification, not be used as definitive claims.
  3. The design simulation assumes exponential survival, proportional hazards, non-informative dropout, and no competing risks, and the evidence comes from one historical trial. The next trial should pre-specify its analysis, include a PH-robust primary or sensitivity analysis, and use the simulation-based sample size rather than a single formula.

Traceability

Every number in this report is read from an artifact produced by the analysis scripts; the report never refits a model. The sources are:

  • results/cohort_summary.csv, results/km_summary.csv, results/cox_hazard_ratios.csv, results/ph_diagnostics.csv, results/concordance_frequentist.csv (frequentist analysis);
  • results/bayes_posterior_summary.csv, results/shrinkage_report.csv, results/model_comparison.csv, results/bayes_convergence.csv (Bayesian analysis);
  • results/power_curve.csv, results/type1_error.csv, results/sample_size_vs_schoenfeld.csv, results/simulation_meta.csv (design simulation);
  • figures/km_by_arm.png, figures/schoenfeld.png, figures/posterior_hr.png, figures/power_curves.png.

The analysis was run with R 4.6.1 and the Bayesian fit used the brms backend (brms with rstan). The full pipeline is reproducible with Rscript scripts/run_all.R; the exact package versions are in results/session_info.txt after a pipeline run.
